title: It 1
subtitle: It's a miracle that she wasn't hurt
summary: Use introductory it to move a long or important part of the sentence to the end, where English prefers it.

lesson.heading: Why we start with it

left.label: Heavy subject at the front
examples: To drive without a licence is illegal.
That she wasn't hurt is a miracle.

right.label: Introductory it - the long or new part comes last
examples: **It is** illegal **to drive** without a licence.

lesson.note: Introductory it also works when the subject is a wh- or -ing clause: It is clear why Diego decided to leave Spain. / It is useless asking Sophie to help.

lesson.heading: it + verb + to-infinitive
lesson.text: A few verbs follow introductory it directly and are then completed by a to-infinitive.

examples.text: 'I've got a terrible headache.' '**It helps to lie** down.'
If you want someone to help you, **it doesn't do to annoy** them just before you ask.

lesson.note: Also: hurt, pay (= give an advantage or benefit).

lesson.heading: it + verb + object + to-infinitive
lesson.text: Most verbs in this pattern are about feelings, and the object usually refers to a person.

examples.text: **It shocked him to see** her looking so ill.
**It means a lot to get** a place at university.

lesson.note: Also: amaze, annoy, astonish, concern, cost, frighten, hurt, scare, surprise, upset, worry.

lesson.heading: It takes ... to ...
lesson.text: We use **it + take + object + to-infinitive** to say what an activity needs - time, resources or personal qualities.

examples.text: **It takes** a lot of effort **to play** the flute.
examples.note: or To play the flute takes a lot of effort.

lesson.heading: it + verb + (object) + that-clause
lesson.text: Verbs of appearing and emerging take it + a that-clause. Several of them can also take an object, which usually refers to a person.

examples.text: **It seems that** she has lost her memory.
examples.note: also appear, come about, follow, happen, transpire

examples.text: **It emerged that** he already had a criminal record.
**It suddenly hit me that** Sara wanted to borrow money.
examples.note: less likely: That Sara wanted to borrow money suddenly hit me. Also dawn on, not bother, strike (= occur to), turn out

lesson.heading: Not with a noun subject - except in speech
lesson.text: We don't normally use an **it ...** pattern instead of a noun as subject. In informal speech, though, this is common when we want to give special emphasis to what comes after it, or to leave a long noun phrase until the end.

examples.text: **It tastes** really good, this new ice cream.
**It's** ridiculous, all the bureaucracy involved in running a school these days.

lesson.text: If the subject is a clause, introductory it almost always improves the sentence; if the subject is just a noun phrase, leave it alone in writing.

exercises.prompt: ___ illegal to drive without a licence.
exercises.explanation: Introductory it lets the to-infinitive clause come at the end.

exercises.prompt: You can save money by booking tickets in advance, so it ___ to plan your journey ahead.
exercises.explanation: it pays to do something = doing it gives you an advantage.

exercises.statement: It is an advantage in the job to be a qualified driver.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The to-infinitive subject moves to the end after it is + noun phrase.

exercises.prompt: Since I broke my ankle last year, it ___ to pedal my bicycle.
exercises.explanation: hurt follows it either with or without an object.

exercises.prompt: I told Peter that I had invited Hugo, too. When he became angry, it ___ that he was jealous.
exercises.explanation: it struck me that ... = the idea suddenly occurred to me.

exercises.prompt: Is the sentence acceptable in written English, or only in informal speech?

items.text: It is highly unusual to put carpet on walls.
It's a Ferrari, Robin's new car.
It was unsettling how he stared straight at me.
It is hard finding a good plumber these days.
It tastes really good, this new ice cream.

exercises.prompt: Children need a lot of praise and it ___ to criticise them too much.
exercises.explanation: it doesn't do to ... = it is not advisable or acceptable to ... .

exercises.prompt: The boys walked towards me in a threatening way, and it ___ to see that they were carrying knives.
exercises.explanation: Verbs of feeling like scare take it + object + to-infinitive.

exercises.statement: It was surprising Francesco's excellent exam result.
exercises.explanation: In writing: Francesco's excellent exam result was surprising. Only in speech would we say 'It was surprising, Francesco's excellent exam result.'

exercises.prompt: I knew that Lotta was a journalist for the local paper, but it ___ to discover that she was also a successful novelist.
exercises.explanation: astonish takes it + object + to-infinitive, and the object refers to a person.

exercises.prompt: Say what playing the flute needs, beginning It takes ... .
exercises.answer: It takes a lot of effort to play the flute.
exercises.explanation: It takes + object + to-infinitive says what an activity requires.

exercises.prompt: There were no curtains in his house, but it ___ that everyone could see in.
exercises.explanation: not bother takes it + object + that-clause, and the object refers to a person.
